statement_en: Is there some $\epsilon>0$ such that there are infinitely many $n$ where all primes $p\leq (2+\epsilon)\log n$ divide\[\prod_{1\leq i\leq \log n}(n+i)?\]

issues: None substantive. The product over integer i with 1 ≤ i ≤ log n is exactly (n+1)⋯(n+⌊log n⌋), as B states.
Natural log is the standard reading in this context.
The conventions for small n (k = 0 when log n < 0, empty product equal to 1) affect only finitely many n. They cannot change an 'infinitely many n' assertion.
The quantifier order (∃ε>0, then infinitely many n, then all primes p ≤ (2+ε) log n) and the non-strict bound p ≤ (2+ε) log n match A.
faithfulness.backtranslation: There exists a real number ε > 0 with the following property: there are infinitely many natural numbers n such that every prime p with p ≤ (2 + ε)·log n divides the product (n+1)(n+2)⋯(n+k), where k = ⌊log n⌋. Here log is the natural logarithm, and k is taken to be 0 when log n < 0. Equivalently, each prime up to (2 + ε)·log n divides at least one of the ⌊log n⌋ consecutive integers n+1, …, n+⌊log n⌋. When ⌊log n⌋ = 0, the product is empty and equals 1.
